meta.titre: Tapeworm Biology: the pork tapeworm, its life cycle and its parasitic way of life
meta.sous_theme: Taenia solium: hosts, life cycle, adaptations and control

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In a village near Bafoussam, a family shares a pig for the end of year feast, and one cut of pork is cooked only lightly over the fire. Weeks later, a member of the family feels hungry all the time yet loses weight, and notices small white segments in the toilet. The cause may be the pork tapeworm, a flatworm that can live in the human intestine for years. The GCE asks about its stages, hosts and adaptations almost every year, so you must be able to tell the story in the right order and explain each feature.

items: A parasite lives on or in another organism, the host, and gets food from it while the host is harmed.
The small intestine is where digested food is absorbed into the blood.
Pigs are domestic animals that can pick up infections from the soil and from faeces.

sections.titre: Taenia solium: hosts, life cycle and adaptations
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Hosts
The pork tapeworm (*Taenia solium*) is a flatworm. The **definitive host** is the human, in whose small intestine the adult lives. The **intermediate host** is the pig, in whose muscles the larva lives.

### Parts of the adult
The head, or **scolex**, carries four suckers and a ring of hooks, and fixes the worm to the intestinal wall. Behind it is a long ribbon of segments called **proglottids**. The oldest segments at the end are full of fertilised eggs and break off.

### Life cycle in order
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | Ripe proglottids with eggs leave the human in the faeces. |
| 2 | A pig swallows eggs on contaminated food or soil. |
| 3 | In the pig's gut each egg hatches into a small larva (oncosphere) with hooks, which bores through the gut wall and is carried by the blood to the muscles. |
| 4 | In the muscle it develops into a **cysticercus**, or bladder worm, with a head folded inside. |
| 5 | A person eats raw or undercooked infected pork. |
| 6 | In the human gut the head turns out, attaches to the wall and grows into a new adult. |

### Adaptations to a parasitic life
| Feature | How it helps |
|---|---|
| Hooks and suckers on the scolex | Hold on against the movement of food in the gut |
| Long, flat body | Large surface area for absorbing food |
| No digestive system | It absorbs ready-digested food from the host's gut through its body surface |
| Thick cuticle and substances that resist enzymes | Protect it from the host's digestive juices |
| Each proglottid has male and female parts | Eggs can be fertilised without meeting another worm |
| Very many eggs | Few eggs will reach a pig, so large numbers raise the chance that some do |
| Respires with little or no oxygen | Oxygen is scarce in the gut |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for a difference between the pork and the beef tapeworm
variantes.contenu_markdown: The beef tapeworm (*Taenia saginata*) has the same life cycle but the intermediate host is cattle, and its scolex has suckers but no hooks. The human is infected by eating raw or undercooked beef.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how infection can be prevented
variantes.contenu_markdown: Cook pork thoroughly. Have meat inspected for cysticerci. Use latrines so that faeces do not reach pig feed or soil. Wash hands, and keep pigs penned and fed on clean food. Treat infected people with prescribed drugs.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks about the harm done by the parasite
variantes.contenu_markdown: The worm takes digested food, so the person may feel hungry and lose weight, and may have abdominal discomfort. If the person swallows the eggs, larvae can develop in tissues such as muscle or brain.

sections.enonce_markdown: Describe how a farmer who has never kept pigs can still become infected with the pork tapeworm, and state two things the farmer could do to avoid infection. *(6 marks)*

etapes.action: Find the key idea in the question
etapes.justification: The question is about how a person becomes infected, so the answer must follow the cycle until the point where the human receives the larva.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The human is the definitive host and gets infected through food or contact with eggs.

etapes.justification: Pigs become infected by eggs and then carry cysticerci in the muscle. A person who buys such pork and eats it badly cooked swallows the larva.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Pig eats eggs, larva forms a cysticercus in the muscle, human eats undercooked pork.

etapes.action: Say what happens in the human gut
etapes.justification: To complete the infection the larva must develop into the adult.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The head turns out, attaches by suckers and hooks to the small intestine and grows into an adult.

etapes.action: Add a second route if relevant
etapes.justification: Eggs from an infected person can also be swallowed through dirty hands or food, so it is not only meat that is a risk.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Eggs swallowed from contaminated hands, water or food can also cause infection.

etapes.justification: Preventive actions must break the cycle at a clear point.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Cook pork thoroughly, and wash hands and use a latrine.

sections.conclusion_markdown: A person who has never kept pigs can become infected by buying and eating pork that contains cysticerci and has been cooked too little to kill them. In the small intestine the head of the larva turns out, attaches itself with suckers and hooks, and grows into an adult worm. A second route is to swallow eggs on dirty hands or contaminated food. The farmer can avoid infection by cooking pork thoroughly and by washing hands after using the toilet and before handling food.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that the adult tapeworm lives in the pig and the larva in the human.
items.pourquoi_faux: The roles are the other way round for the pork tapeworm. The adult lives in the human gut; the larva (cysticercus) lives in the pig's muscle.
items.correction_markdown: Adult: human small intestine (definitive host). Larva: pig muscle (intermediate host).

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that a tapeworm has a mouth and a gut to digest the host's food.
items.pourquoi_faux: A tapeworm has no digestive system. It absorbs food that the host has already digested.
items.correction_markdown: It absorbs digested food through its body surface.

items.erreur_markdown: Answering an adaptation question by describing the life cycle.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question asks how structures and habits suit a parasite. A description of stages earns few marks.
items.correction_markdown: Name a feature, then say how it helps the parasite survive: 'hooks and suckers hold it on against the flow of food'.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving 'eggs' as the stage found in pig muscle.
items.pourquoi_faux: Eggs leave in faeces and hatch in the pig's gut. The stage in muscle is the cysticercus (bladder worm).

items.enonce_markdown: Arrange these stages of the pork tapeworm in the correct order, starting with the adult in the human: cysticercus in pig muscle; eggs swallowed by a pig; adult in the human gut; ripe proglottids leave in faeces; human eats undercooked pork; larva bores through the pig's gut wall.
items.solution_markdown:
1. Adult in the human gut. 2. Ripe proglottids leave in faeces. 3. Eggs swallowed by a pig. 4. Larva bores through the pig's gut wall. 5. Cysticercus in pig muscle. 6. Human eats undercooked pork.

**Order: adult, proglottids in faeces, eggs swallowed by pig, larva bores through gut wall, cysticercus in muscle, human eats undercooked pork.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why (a) a tapeworm can live in the small intestine without being digested, and (b) it needs no digestive system of its own.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) It has a thick cuticle that resists the host's digestive enzymes, and it makes substances that work against those enzymes, so it is not digested.

(b) The host has already digested the food into small soluble molecules such as glucose and amino acids. The long, flat body has a large surface area, so the worm can absorb them directly through its body surface.

**It resists digestion by its cuticle, and it absorbs ready-digested food, so it needs no gut.**

items.enonce_markdown: A health officer says that a whole community can be protected from the pork tapeworm without any drug. (a) Name three actions the community can take. (b) For each action, say which stage of the life cycle it stops. (c) Why does a single worm release so many eggs even though only a few will ever reach a pig?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) and (b)

- Cooking pork thoroughly: kills the cysticercus, so no adult develops in the human.
- Using latrines and washing hands: stops eggs from leaving the human and reaching soil, water, food or pig feed.
- Keeping pigs penned and fed on clean food, with meat inspection: prevents eggs being swallowed by pigs and stops infected meat from reaching people.

(c) The eggs have only a small chance of being eaten by a pig, so a very large number gives a better chance that some will complete the cycle. **Large numbers of eggs compensate for the low chance of each reaching the intermediate host.**

items_markdown: The adult pork tapeworm lives in the human small intestine (definitive host); the larva, a cysticercus, lives in the muscle of the pig (intermediate host).
Life cycle: adult, proglottids with eggs in faeces, eggs swallowed by pig, larva to muscle as cysticercus, human eats undercooked pork, adult.
The scolex has suckers and hooks for attachment; the body is a ribbon of proglottids.
Adaptations: hooks and suckers, flat body, no gut, thick cuticle, hermaphrodite segments, many eggs.
Prevention: cook pork thoroughly, meat inspection, latrines, hand washing, and keeping pigs on clean food.
